turns.content: Hey so I finally figured out why my OD600 readings were all over the place on Saturday — like 0.18 to 0.42 across identical controls 💀 turns out the microcentrifuge tubes were warming up on the bench before I added the TCA, so residual substrate turnover was still happening. Crazy how such a tiny procedural thing can wreck an entire day's work. Anyway, I'm looking at our method sheet now and it says "place tubes on crushed ice prior to 4°C microcentrifugation" — does that confirm my read? Like the ice step is actually essential to stop the reaction, not just a convenience thing? Also the protocol mentions pre-cooling the centrifuge rotor but that feels like a distraction, right?

Yeah, your read is right — and honestly that's a satisfying catch, even if it cost you a Saturday. A 0.18–0.42 spread on identical controls screams "reaction kept running longer in some tubes than others," and bench warming is a classic culprit. Substrate turnover continuing for even a few extra minutes per tube, with variable timing between samples, gives you exactly that kind of scatter.

**On the ice step:** yes, it's essential, not convenience. Until the TCA actually denatures your enzyme, the reaction is still going. Ice drops the rate dramatically (Q10 effects alone — most enzyme rates roughly halve per 10°C drop — plus whatever you're slowing via substrate diffusion), which compresses the error introduced by inconsistent timing between tubes. It's basically a pre-quench so that the *actual* quench happens under controlled, uniform conditions. Your method sheet putting it in writing is the lab encoding someone else's bad Saturday into protocol.

**On the pre-cooled rotor:** not a distraction, don't skip it. If you've quenched with TCA, the chemistry is stopped, so temperature matters less for the reaction itself — but a warm rotor can partially resolubilize or smear your precipitate, and protein pellets are notoriously happier staying cold. A rotor that's been sitting at room temp can take a surprisingly long time to equilibrate to 4°C, so "set to 4°C" ≠ "is at 4°C." Since you're pelleting precipitated protein, you want that pellet tight and cold.

One extra thought: if timing consistency was part of your problem, stagger your TCA additions at fixed intervals (e.g., 30 seconds apart, same interval as your reaction starts) so every tube gets identical reaction time regardless of processing order. That plus strict icing should tighten your controls right up.

Curious what the actual assay is, if you feel like sharing — colorimetric read at 600 after TCA precipitation sounds like it might be a turbidity-based thing rather than a true growth OD?

So the ice step is definitely a real quench then, not just protocol theater 😂 — that's what I was hoping to hear. And good point about the rotor being warm causing pellet smearing, I wouldn't have thought of that. The stagger idea is smart too, I'll set a timer for that.

It's actually a succinate dehydrogenase assay using PMS as the electron mediator, reading reduced INT formazan at 490 — the OD600 was just me checking bacterial growth before harvesting. The TCA precip is for a separate protein normalization step.

Anyway, knowing the ice step locks in the quench timing... that was the missing piece from Saturday. Feels good to have it nailed down

Ah, that context actually changes one thing worth flagging — and I'd hate for you to walk away with a false sense of closure on the wrong variable.

If the 0.18–0.42 scatter was in your **OD600 growth readings themselves** (taken pre-harvest, before any TCA), then tubes warming on the bench can't explain it — the TCA quench step happens downstream and has no way to affect a reading you already took. Warming *would* explain scatter in the final normalized SDH activity values, since turnover continuing pre-quench inflates some tubes' formazan signal relative to their true biomass. But if the raw growth ODs were bouncing around, something else is going on: inconsistent resuspension before reading (cells settle fast — even 2–3 minutes sitting gives you a gradient), condensation on the cuvette, or actual growth differences between the controls.

So the diagnostic question: was the scatter in the raw OD600s, or in the 490 signal / normalized activity? If it's the latter, your Saturday theory holds completely. If it's the former, the ice fix is still correct and worth doing, but there's a second gremlin to hunt — and resuspension technique is my prime suspect.

On the assay itself: SDH + PMS/INT at 490 is a solid setup. One thing to keep in mind given your quench-timing lesson — the PMS-mediated INT reduction is light- and oxygen-sensitive, so keep reactions in the dark or under foil and standardize your read time after stopping, or you'll reintroduce the same class of timing error through the back door. INT formazan also loves to precipitate if it accumulates too much, so make sure you're in the linear range with your protein amounts.

Sounds like Saturday's pain converts into a much tighter method sheet either way. Those are the failures that actually earn their keep.

Wait so you're saying the scatter was in the raw OD600s themselves before any TCA was even added 🤔 honestly that's a really good catch and now I'm second-guessing myself a bit

I was so sure it was the bench warming thing but you're right, if the growth readings were already bouncing around before harvest then the quench step can't be the cause of that initial variance... ugh

The 0.18-0.42 was definitely in the raw OD600 readings before harvest, not the formazan signal. So maybe I still have another gremlin to find? Though honestly the ice fix still feels right for the downstream assay consistency

What do you think about resuspension being the culprit? I was vortexing each tube right before reading but maybe not long enough or consistently

Resuspension is a solid suspect, but let me widen the net slightly because there's a twist that might actually *redeem* part of your original theory.

First — your bench warming idea isn't entirely dead, it just needs reframing. If the OD600 readings were taken from aliquots that sat on the bench for *variable amounts of time* before you read them, the cells kept dividing during that window. Ten extra minutes on the bench at late-exponential growth can easily move an OD by 20–30%. So the mechanism wouldn't be "TCA quench failure" — it'd be "uncontrolled growth time before the reading." Same root cause (bench warming), different victim. Worth asking yourself: was the delay between pulling each sample and reading it consistent?

Now, the resuspension angle — a few specifics, because "vortexed before reading" can still go wrong several ways:

- **Bubbles.** This is my prime suspect, actually. Vigorous vortexing introduces microbubbles, and bubbles scatter 600nm light just like cells do. If you vortex and immediately pour into the cuvette and read, you're measuring cells + a random number of bubbles. Vortex, then give it 10–15 seconds for the foam to clear, and be consistent about that delay.
- **Settling during batch reads.** If you vortex tube 1, then tube 2, then tube 3... and *then* read them all, tube 1 has been settling for minutes by the time it's read. Vortex each tube immediately before *its* reading, not in a batch ahead of time.
- **Cuvette handling.** Fingerprints, condensation on cold cuvettes, and rotational orientation (always face the same cuvette side toward the beam — cheap cuvettes have measurable orientation-dependent scatter) all add noise, especially at low OD where your signal-to-noise is already thin.

One more thing to check: at ODs of 0.18–0.42 you're in a fine linear range, so that's not it — but if these were genuinely parallel identical cultures, don't fully rule out that the growth differences were *real* (inoculum volume variation, position effects in the incubator/shaker). A quick test: grow one culture, split it into 12 tubes, and read all 12 with your standard technique. The spread on that tells you your measurement noise floor. Anything above that in real experiments is biology, not pipetting.

And yes — keep the ice fix regardless. It solves the downstream normalization problem even if it turns out not to have been Saturday's villain.

Hmm so I'm thinking I should add a note to the lab binder about this for my rotation student Priya — she starts next week and I don't want her repeating my Saturday nightmare 😅 Do you think the ice fix would generalize to other assays in the binder, or is it pretty specific to TCA precipitation protocols

The ice principle generalizes really well — it's less a TCA-specific trick and more a family of the same underlying rule: *any enzymatic process continues until you actively stop it, and cold is your cheapest brake.* For the binder note, I'd frame it that way so Priya learns the principle, not just the one step.

Where it applies across a typical methods binder:

- **Any stopped enzymatic assay with a quench reagent** (TCA, perchloric acid, NaOH, boiling, whatever) — the ice step before the quench matters the same way. The quench has a dead time between "reagent added" and "enzyme actually dead," and cold compresses the error from inconsistent timing during that window.
- **Cell lysis and protein extraction** — ice isn't optional there at all; proteases and phosphatases wake up the moment you break cells open. If your binder has any lysate prep, that one's already hopefully explicit, but it reinforces the pattern.
- **Subcellular fractionation / organelle preps** — everything cold, always, including tubes and rotors (the warm-rotor point from earlier applies here too).
- **RNA work** — arguably the extreme case; RNases don't even wait politely.

Where it *doesn't* transfer, so she doesn't over-apply it:

- **Live-cell / growth measurements** — cold shocks some organisms and you don't want to freeze your reading conditions. Different fix there (consistent timing, not ice).
- **Assays where the "stop" is instantaneous and complete on addition** (strong denaturant straight into the reaction at high concentration, flash-freezing) — the pre-chill matters less because there's no dead time to compress.
- **Enzymes that cold-inactivate or cold-dissociate** — rare, but they exist, and chilling pre-quench would bias the measurement itself. Worth a line in the note that if she's ever adapting this to a new enzyme, check that the enzyme tolerates cold first.

For the note itself, I'd keep it to three lines: the principle (reaction runs until quenched; ice minimizes pre-quench drift), the mechanics (ice before quench, stagger additions at fixed intervals, pre-cool the rotor), and one honest sentence about Saturday — "controls varied 0.18–0.42 when this was skipped" is worth more than any amount of abstract instruction. Rotation students remember cautionary tales way better than rules.

Want me to draft the actual binder note text? Happy to write it up in a format you can just paste in.

That makes sense — cold as a general brake rather than just a protocol quirk. I think I'll write it up this afternoon while it's fresh. Thanks for talking through it with me, I feel way more confident about Wednesday's run now

Glad it helped — you've got a solid plan for Wednesday: ice before quench, staggered additions, consistent vortex-and-settle on the OD reads, and that split-culture noise-floor test if you want to be thorough. Honestly, the fact that a bad Saturday turned into a better protocol *and* a teaching note for Priya is about the best possible outcome from a wrecked experiment.

Good luck with the run — hope the controls behave themselves this time 🔬
